title: "What Drives House Prices in Ames, Iowa?"
subtitle: "Log-linear regression, diagnostics and regularization on the Ames Housing data"

  freeze: false  # always re-read the results saved by the analysis pages
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("R/setup.R")
eda <- readRDS(file.path("results", "eda.rds"))
mod <- readRDS(file.path("results", "models.rds"))
ev <- function(model, metric) mod$eval_table[model, metric]
ols <- "Log model, smearing"
```

This project explains and predicts the sale prices of
`r fmt_num(eda$n_sales)` houses sold in Ames, Iowa, between
`r eda$years[1]` and `r eda$years[2]`. It estimates which characteristics of a
house move its price, tests whether the regression assumptions hold, and
measures how accurately the model prices houses it has not seen, in dollars.

## Key results

- **The model prices new houses within about `r fmt_pct(ev(ols, "MAPE"), 0)`
  on average.** On a held-out test set of `r fmt_num(mod$n_test)` houses, the
  mean absolute error is `r fmt_usd(ev(ols, "MAE"))` and the model explains
  `r fmt_pct(ev(ols, "R2"), 0)` of the price variation, against
  `r fmt_usd(ev("Simple regression", "MAE"))` and
  `r fmt_pct(ev("Simple regression", "R2"), 0)` for living area alone.
- **Quality, size and location drive prices.** Each step on the 10-level
  quality scale adds about `r fmt_pct(mod$effects["quality"], 0)`, a 10%
  larger house costs about `r fmt_pct(1.1^mod$effects["area_elasticity"] - 1)`
  more, and the same house costs about
  `r fmt_pct((1 + mod$nb_high$effect) / (1 + mod$nb_low$effect) - 1, 0)` more
  in `r mod$nb_high$neighborhood` than in `r mod$nb_low$neighborhood`.
- **Room counts add little once size is known**: their effects are small and
  not robust, and the simpler Lasso model drops them.
- **Ridge and Lasso do not beat OLS** here: with
  `r fmt_num(mod$n_train)` training houses and moderate multicollinearity, the
  OLS estimates are already stable.
- **The largest errors come from unusual sales.** Only
  `r fmt_pct(mod$extreme["share_normal"], 0)` of the houses with extreme
  residuals were normal sales, against
  `r fmt_pct(mod$extreme["share_normal_all"], 0)` overall: foreclosures, family
  sales and unfinished houses sell far from their modeled value.

## What the analysis covers

- [Data and EDA](data-eda.qmd): variable selection, descriptive statistics,
  distributions and correlations, the log transform, a stratified 70/30
  train/test split, and an exploratory segmentation with K-Means and PCA.
- [Models](models.qmd): simple and multiple OLS regression with percentage
  interpretation of log coefficients; RESET, Breusch-Pagan, Durbin-Watson and
  Jarque-Bera tests; robust and clustered standard errors; VIF; outliers and
  Cook's distance; test-set evaluation in dollars with Duan's smearing
  correction; scenario forecasts with normal and empirical prediction
  intervals; Ridge and Lasso with cross-validation.
- [Conclusions](conclusions.qmd): findings, weaknesses of the model, uses in
  property valuation and credit risk, limitations and extensions.

All numbers in the text are computed in R when the report is rendered. The
code is on [GitHub](https://github.com/xwmara/house-price-regression).

## Data

The data are the Ames Housing data of De Cock (2011), in the processed version
of the [AmesHousing](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=AmesHousing) R package.

De Cock, D. (2011). Ames, Iowa: Alternative to the Boston Housing Data as an
End of Semester Regression Project. *Journal of Statistics Education*, 19(3).
<https://doi.org/10.1080/10691898.2011.11889627>
